Back to the value on PS4.

Switches all settings on this tab and the texture pack at once, live. Stock is the game as shipped; Recommended is the default. Your own presets are files in the presets folder, also listed in the launcher.
Saves the current settings under this name (an existing preset with the name is replaced).
Deletes the selected preset file. The settings stay as they are.
Windowed, borderless window or exclusive fullscreen.
Waits for the monitor: no tearing, a little more input delay.
The game's own HDR10 output, used when HDR is on in Windows display settings. Applies after a restart.
Shows one made-up image between two game frames: smoother motion, a little more input delay. DLSS needs NVIDIA RTX 40 or newer; FSR is not tied to one brand.
Off now: the game runs at 30 FPS (frame rate mode or Frame rate limit), too low for frame generation. Your choice comes back at a higher frame rate.
With VSync on, the screen's refresh rate must be at least twice the game's frame rate.
Sharpens the image. Now done by the anti-aliasing step itself (its RCAS), on the scene only.
Sharpens the image. With Built-in it is AMD CAS on the final picture; with DLSS, FSR or TAA their own sharpening.
How strong the sharpening is. Up to 100%: the upscaler's own sharpening; every 100% above adds one more sharpening pass.
How strong the sharpening is. CAS stops at 100%.

How the image gets its size. Off: drawn at the screen's size. Built-in, DLSS, FSR 3.1 and FSR 4: drawn smaller and enlarged, for more speed; DLSS needs an NVIDIA RTX card, FSR 4 any recent card (not only AMD; sharper and steadier than FSR 3.1), FSR 3.1 runs on any card, Built-in is the game's own upscale pass. An upscaler also smooths the edges itself. F8 switches between Built-in and your choice in game.
Until the restart the game keeps rendering at %dx
Output / 1.5 (Quality), 1.7 (Balanced), 2 (Performance) or 3 (Ultra Performance) per side; the upscaler fills in the rest. Set at start, so changing it needs Apply and restart.

Smooths jagged edges. Yours to choose with Upscale method Off; an upscaler does its own. DLAA (NVIDIA RTX cards) and FSR 4 (any recent card) are the sharpest, FSR 3.1 runs on any card, TAA is lighter and softer. Off keeps only the game's own.

Smooths jagged edges (feathers, grass, railings) on the final image. The game draws its HUD and subtitles into the same image, so text edges are smoothed too. About 0.2 to 0.4 ms per frame at 1080p (RTX 2060).

Draws the shadow maps at 2x or 4x the game's 2048x2048 (default: Game). The main gain is much less shimmer of tree and leaf shadows, with any anti-aliasing. 8192 costs about 8 FPS and up to about 2 GB of video memory (4096 about a quarter of that). With 8 GB of video memory or less keep Game: running out causes stutter and crashes.
Camera field of view. Default 70° is as shipped; higher shows more around the boy. Applies while the game runs (not in the paused menu).
Strength of the contact shadows in corners and under grass. 0% turns the pass off (saves a little GPU time). Above 150% the half-resolution AO shows blocky halos.
Glow around bright light. 0% turns the pass off.
Reflections and light glare on water and wet stone. 0% turns the pass off.
Camera motion blur. 0% turns the pass off.
Darkened screen corners. The game ships with this off: 0% is as shipped and recommended.
The game's own sharpening filter. On by default: 100% is the original and the maximum (recommended).
Where the fog starts and reaches full strength. Default 100% is as shipped; lower brings the fog closer.

The game's chromatic aberration on the light haze: yellow and blue edges around objects against fog, strongest toward the screen edges. Sharp anti-aliasing (DLAA, DLSS) makes it stand out more. Default 0% gives clean edges; 100% is as shipped.
The game moves most grass only every 4th frame, which looks choppy at high frame rates. Every frame (default) moves it smoothly.
How strongly the wind moves the boy's hair and clothing. Default 100% is as shipped and can look like a storm; 50% is recommended, 30% is calm.
How strongly the wind moves trees, leaves and ivy. Default 100% is as shipped; 50% looks more natural (recommended), 0% keeps them still.
How strongly the wind moves Trico's feathers. Default 100% is as shipped; 0% keeps them still.

Sharper (below 0) or softer (above 0) scene textures under DLAA; no effect without DLAA. -1.00 is NVIDIA's advice for native resolution. Lower brings out fine detail, mostly on grass (-3.00 has 31% more fine detail than +1.00), but can shimmer in motion.

Keeps ground and wall textures sharp at shallow angles. The game uses trilinear and 4x. In our tests (a stone path, a pillar hall) 16x looked the same as Game; it stays on because the cost is very small.

AI-upscaled versions of the game's textures, made from your own copy of the game (ps4-texturepack-generator, docs/texture-pack.md); the game files are not changed. Switches live; textures appear as they load (a second or two).
Brightness, contrast, saturation and gamma of the final image (the HUD included). SDR only; HDR is left as is. Default on, all neutral (gamma 1); off is the game as shipped. No measurable cost.
Adds light or shadow evenly; 0 is unchanged.
Spreads tones away from mid gray; 1 is unchanged.
Color intensity: 0 is black and white, 1 is unchanged.
Above 1 lightens the midtones, below 1 darkens them; blacks and whites stay. Default 1, the game's own; 0.75 tames the over-lit SDR image outdoors.
No rows in the TLG_LAB file.
Start with port\tools\jitter\start.cmd for the lab rows (TLG_LAB).
Fixed rows back to their defaults, lab rows back to the game's values.
Ctrl+click a slider to type a value. The right column is the game's own value (the part the row changes). Rows change the game's objects every 15 frames and follow area changes; pausing stops them.
Caps the presented frames. The game runs at 30 FPS (as on PS4); 60 FPS is a launcher option.
Caps the presented frames. 60 FPS mode (launcher): limits above 60 have no effect.
Caps the presented frames. Unlocked mode (launcher): Unlimited follows the display refresh, up to 120.
More frames queued: steadier FPS, slower response to input.
When the game reads GPU-written memory, also copy back the other GPU-written data around it. Off is fastest (2-5 FPS more in tests); 64 MB is not recommended.

Fixes a known bug of the game at 60 FPS and unlocked: two slow-motion moments turn choppy and can freeze the game. The same bug made the PS4 60 FPS patches freeze here. The moments: the jump to Trico's tail (s06_FallingBridge, cutscene fb_110) and the collapsing bridge (s10_Pit). Issues #39 and #40. At 30 FPS nothing changes. Applies when the scene starts.

After each stage or checkpoint load, frees the textures of earlier stages that the new one does not use. Without it they stay in video memory until it runs short. In one test it kept 69 FPS where the game had dropped to 57 after 28 loads, but in a longer test the game still got slower over many loads (issue #20), so it is off by default for now. Off is the emulator's original behaviour.

Keeps a texture the GPU drew into while its only correct copy is on the GPU (a game write right next to it blocks the copy back), until video memory is almost full. Without it, cleanup can throw that picture away and the game gets old data back. From SpartanPort (@maze1377). On by default; turn it off if video memory runs full more often.
Debug: give back freed buffer memory

Since v0.5.2: when the game frees memory, its graphics card copy goes too. Test switch (issue #38): turn it off to check whether a problem started with v0.5.2. Off is the behaviour before v0.5.2. From the Shadow of the Colossus PC port (@AjncSystem, @Oussama268).
Debug: texture cleanup follows the driver

Since v0.5.2: texture cleanup starts at the video memory the driver offers now, never below the start-up limits. Test switch (issue #38): off uses only the start-up limits (the behaviour before v0.5.2), so textures are cleaned up sooner.
The performance overlay in a corner of the screen.
Items side by side or stacked.
Where the game's sound goes. Applies at the next start; an unplugged device falls back to the system default.
Sends all 8 channels even to a stereo device. Turn on for Windows Sonic or Dolby Atmos for Headphones (headphone surround). Off: stereo devices get a stereo mix. Applies at the next start.
The game window takes the mouse while it has focus. Esc releases it; a click in the window takes it back.
How far the camera turns for the same mouse movement.
Moving the mouse forward looks down.
Evens out the camera motion; higher values feel softer and a little slower.
Fast movements turn more than slow ones. 0 is linear.
Small mouse movements skip the game's stick dead zone. Raise it if slow movements do nothing.
Set: press and hold two or more buttons together, then let go. Keyboard: Alt+Q quits, Insert opens this menu.
E or middle click / Left Shift
Remap keys and mouse buttons in the launcher (Controls); it applies at the next start.

Starts the stage at this point, as the game's own level select does. The story continues from there, and the game can save there at its next checkpoint: keep a copy of your save (launcher: Saves folder) if you want to go back.

A new Trico appears next to the boy. At most 8 extra: with more, the game's physics runs out of room and the game crashes. For fun only: they do not follow the story and can block the way. A jump or another stage ends them.

The world stands still and you fly the camera to take a picture. Left stick: fly. Right stick: look around. L2 / R2: down / up. Hold R1: fast, hold L1: slow. Cross or Print Screen: save a screenshot to user/screenshots. L3 + R3, F9 (or this menu) turns it on and off. A jump turns it off.

How the world is frozen. Pause the game: the game's own pause, everything stops. Stop time: the game's own slow motion, turned down until nothing moves; try it if the camera does not move with the first one.

Trico drives himself: he wanders the scene, looks for edges to climb or jump, and the camera follows him. It is the developers' own debug tool, still in the game. They used it to leave the game running by itself for hours: their script can even walk him on to the next scene and knows every stage's start points, their own version of a soak test. Three of its pieces say how old it is: a line to restart the game over a network socket from a PC called D:\trico, a camera preset named TricoAutoRunTest_middle, and helper volumes that are not even on the disc any more (the game quietly skips those, which is why he sometimes picks an odd route). Turning it off gives you the camera and Trico back. For fun only: he ignores the story, he can wander into water or into a load trigger, and the story keeps running around him.
Gives Trico and the camera back to you. He stops where he stands, and the normal camera follows the boy again.

Near keeps Trico big in the picture and is the best of the four in open scenes. Middle is the one the developers' tool picks itself: a classic top-down view, but in a narrow or roofed place the camera can end up inside the rock. Far looks down on the whole area, which is lovely in a valley and useless indoors, because Trico becomes a dot. Game camera leaves your normal camera alone: it keeps following the boy while Trico wanders off on his own.
Trico's eyes keep changing to random colours: the game's own hidden effect, normally only seen in a few story moments. Turning it off brings the normal colours back. A jump turns it off.

Unlocks every treasure (outfits, Trico's feathers) and the Treasures entry in the options menu, with the developers' own unlock. Stored in your save: turning it off does not take them back. Your saves are backed up before the first unlock (the launcher's save manager can restore them). Select them in the game's pause menu, under Items.
The boy wears horns, a nod to Ico. Can be combined with the game's own Ico outfit (one of the treasures). Turn it on in the launcher once first: the launcher builds the horn models on your PC.
Turn on ICO horns in the launcher (Mods page) once first.
L1 / R1 or Q / E: switch tabs. Settings are saved in tlg.ini.
